content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Graphify Incremental Merge Workflow

Graphify can be run incrementally — processing a single new document and merging its extracted nodes into an existing knowledge graph rather than rebuilding the graph from scratch. On 2026-06-11, a product roadmap course note (~1,405 words) was processed by graphify for the KeystoneOS project, extracting 29 nodes that were merged into the existing graph, growing it from 61 to 90 nodes, 140 to 173 edges, and maintaining 9 semantic communities. Trace results are stored in `graphify-out\memory\` for future `--update` queryability, and a PowerShell quoting gotcha was discovered and resolved. On 2026-06-17, a full meetings corpus run (78 documents) surfaced two additional lessons applicable to all graphify runs: chunk output truncation recovery and entity deduplication failure when bare first names are present in an organizational corpus.

## Key Points

- **Incremental merge, not full rebuild:** graphify supports adding new source material to an existing graph without reprocessing the entire corpus. The merge integrates newly extracted nodes and edges into the existing graph structure, with community detection re-run on the merged result.
- **2026-06-11 growth metrics:** 61 → 90 nodes (+29), 140 → 173 edges (+33), 9 communities maintained. Input was a ~1,405 word product roadmap course note.
- **Bridge nodes reveal cross-community insights:** the `Adoption Is the Bottleneck` node bridges two distinct communities (Roadmap Process & Alignment ↔ Roadmap Strategy & Prioritization) because the underlying note explicitly links the milestone-selection rule (target adoption barriers) to both strategic planning and execution alignment — a non-obvious structural connection made visible in the graph.
- **Trace results saved to `graphify-out\memory\`:** the rationale behind bridge relationships is saved for future `--update` queryability, making the graph's reasoning auditable and extensible across sessions.
- **PowerShell inline script quoting gotcha:** when constructing graphify merge commands in PowerShell, inline scripts (JSON payloads, multi-line arguments, strings with special characters) are mangled by PowerShell's quoting rules. The fix: write complex content to a temp file first, then reference the file path in the command.
- **Chunk output truncation recovery (2026-06-17):** graphify processes large corpora in chunks; output can be truncated mid-stream at token limits. Salvage approach: extract nodes and edges arrays from markdown-fenced and partial JSON content produced before the truncation point. On 2026-06-17 this recovered 142/142 nodes and 171/197 edges (87%) from a truncated chunk without re-running the full chunk. Re-running is not always necessary when node completeness is high.
- **Entity deduplication — first-name ambiguity in orgs (2026-06-17):** bare first-name nodes are unreliable targets for speculative semantic merging in organizational corpora with multiple professionals sharing common first names. In the 2026-06-17 meetings corpus, Tyler, Kevin, and Cody each resolved to 2 distinct people (Tyler Held / Tyler Wright, Kevin Robinson / Kevin Washington, Cody Soto / Cody Hall). False `semantically_similar_to` merges must be removed; always confirm first-name disambiguation with the user before merging.

## Details

The incremental merge workflow is architecturally distinct from a full-corpus rebuild. Rather than re-ingesting all source documents, graphify processes a single new document, extracts its semantic entities and relationships, and merges them into the existing graph's node and edge set. This makes the workflow practical for large, growing knowledge graphs: each new document takes seconds to process and merge while the accumulated graph structure grows organically. The trace artifact saved to `graphify-out\memory\` records the provenance of bridge relationships — which source material linked which previously-disconnected communities — enabling future graph traversal to explain why two concepts are structurally connected. Saving traces is especially valuable for incrementally built graphs where the rationale for any given edge may span multiple source documents added in separate sessions.

The PowerShell quoting issue is a Windows-specific friction point in the graphify workflow. PowerShell's argument-handling rules for complex string arguments differ from bash's rules: JSON payloads, multi-line strings, and arguments containing double quotes, backslashes, or special characters are subject to nested escape sequences that mangle the intended content when passed inline. The reliable pattern is to write the complex content to a temporary `.json` or `.txt` file and reference that file by path in the graphify command. This sidesteps PowerShell's quoting rules entirely — the file is read raw, without shell interpolation — and matches the same principle documented for hook scripts in [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]: prefer file-based argument passing over inline strings when the shell's quoting semantics would transform the content.

Chunk output truncation is a reliability concern for any graphify run over a large corpus or a single long document that generates substantial output. The salvage approach works because graphify's output format is structured: nodes and edges are output as JSON arrays within markdown code fences. Content before the truncation point is often well-formed even if the overall output is incomplete. Extracting the nodes object and edges object from pre-truncation content yields a partial but usable graph segment. The decision to accept partial recovery vs. re-run the full chunk depends on the ratio of recovered to total edges and the sensitivity of the analysis to missing relationships. For most exploratory knowledge graph use cases, 85-90% edge recovery is sufficient. For the full-corpus meetings case, see [[concepts/graphify-meetings-corpus-analysis]] for the specific recovery metrics and the additional entity deduplication challenges that arise at corpus scale.

# Backup Manifest Drift and Stale launchd Exit Status

On 2026-08-31 a `/claude-stack-doctor` health check investigated a failed 09:00 `com.keystone.dailybackup` run and traced it to three project folders missing from the hand-maintained backup manifest. The manifest was corrected at 10:31, the backup re-ran immediately and completed with 0 errors, but `launchctl list` continued to report a non-zero exit code because that column reflects only the last *scheduled* run. The session established both a new failure mode (manifest omission, distinct from the documented `backup-*` classes) and a diagnostic rule for reading launchd status against the backup log timeline.

## Key Points

- **Manifest omission is its own failure class.** Three project folders were absent from the backup manifest; the job surfaced this as `backup-error` with per-folder entries in `daily-backup.log`, not as any of the previously documented `backup-*` failure classes.
- **`launchctl list` column 2 reports the last *scheduled* run only.** Manual or out-of-band re-runs do not update it, so a green `daily-backup.log` and a red launchd status can coexist without contradiction.
- **Confirm against the log timeline before treating an exit code as live.** The correct ground truth for "is the backup healthy right now?" is the most recent run's log entry, not the launchd status field.
- **A stale exit code is left to self-clear.** The recommendation was to do nothing rather than force-run the job: the next 09:00 scheduled run overwrites the status, and a manual re-run would change only the cosmetic field, not any real state.
- **Hand-maintained manifests drift.** The recorded follow-up question is whether the manifest should be auto-derived from `~/.claude/projects` rather than curated by hand, removing the omission failure mode at its source.

## Details

The manifest omission is a coverage failure rather than an execution failure, which is why it does not fit the existing `backup-*` taxonomy. Every path the job was told to back up succeeded; the defect is that three paths were never in the instruction set. This class is silent by construction — a backup whose scope is wrong still reports per-folder success for the folders it knows about, and only the aggregate `backup-error` plus the per-folder entries in `daily-backup.log` expose the gap. The proposed remedy of deriving the manifest from `~/.claude/projects` rather than maintaining it by hand converts an omission that requires human vigilance into one that requires a directory scan, which is the same move as replacing an inferred boundary with a declared one elsewhere in this stack.

The launchd status lag is a distinct lesson about which signal counts as ground truth. `launchctl list` exposes the exit status of the daemon's own last invocation of the job, so any run initiated outside the schedule — a manual invocation, an interactive re-run during a diagnostic session — leaves that field untouched. The consequence is a persistent false-red: the system is healthy, the log proves it, and the status field will disagree until the next scheduled tick. The correct response is to read the status field as a timestamped historical claim and reconcile it against the backup log's timeline, exactly as background-task exit codes must be reconciled against on-disk artifacts before being believed. Force-running the job to clear the field would be treating the display as the state.

Both findings reinforce that this backup subsystem accumulates its failures at the reporting layer rather than the data layer. The snapshots themselves were fine in the 2026-08-06 receipt-race incident, fine here after the manifest fix, and the recurring diagnostic work is about which of several disagreeing signals — receipt read-back, launchd exit code, per-folder log entries — actually describes the backup's state.

# Handoff Document Placement: Never Write to /tmp

On 2026-08-15, a session resuming work on the portfolio board project could not locate its handoff document. A search of the entire home directory — six levels deep, excluding `Library` and `node_modules` — turned up nothing. The file had been written by the prior session to `/tmp/`, which is invisible to a home-directory search and is wiped on reboot. The handoff was copied to `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/handoff-portfolio-board-task4-2026-08-15.md`, establishing the rule that handoff documents belong in the project directory.

## Key Points

- **`/tmp/` is doubly wrong for handoffs:** the file does not survive a reboot, and it is outside the search path a fresh session would naturally check (a home-directory sweep). Either failure alone loses the document; together they make the loss silent.
- **Write handoffs into the project directory.** The recovered file now lives at `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/`, alongside the work it describes, where both a filesystem search and a repository listing will find it.
- **When a handoff cannot be found, ask the user for the *project name*, not the file path.** The project name is something the user reliably knows and it localizes the search immediately; a path the user must reconstruct from memory is slower and often wrong.
- **A near-limit session should not start work it cannot finish.** Task 4 was deliberately not begun: it requires spawning implementer and reviewer subagents over a long run, and the usage limit was close. Starting and being cut off mid-run was judged worse than not starting at all.
- **State at handoff:** Tasks 1–3 done, pushed, 59 tests passing. Work happens in the worktree `~/DEV/project-triage/.claude/worktrees/portfolio-merge-editor`, not the main folder. Task 4 is to make `save_registry` atomic (temp-file write plus swap), with code and two regression tests already specified in the plan file. Tasks 5–10 follow the same one-subagent-per-task loop; the final merge to `master` has a known conflict requiring a user decision.

## Details

The failure mode here is specific to ephemeral system directories and is worth stating precisely: a handoff document's entire purpose is to survive the boundary between sessions, so writing it to a location defined by the operating system as not surviving boundaries defeats it categorically. `/tmp` is an attractive default for an agent writing a scratch file — it is always writable and requires no decision about where the file belongs — but a handoff is not scratch output. The recovery in this case depended on the user having the prior session's tool output available to paste; without that, the file's location was unrecoverable by search, because the search space a fresh session reasons about is the home directory and the project tree, not the system temp directory. The generalizable rule is that any artifact whose value is realized in a *later* session must be written where a later session will look, which in practice means the project directory or a durable notes location — the same reasoning that put the machine-restore handoff into a committed `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` path in [[concepts/machine-restore-closeout-handoff]] rather than anywhere transient.

The retrieval lesson is a small but reusable debugging heuristic. When a search for a named file fails, the instinct is to widen the search or ask the user to confirm the filename. Both are slow: widening a home-directory sweep costs time and still misses `/tmp`, and a user asked for a file path will frequently supply an approximation. Asking instead for the *project name* changes the query from "where is this file" to "which tree should I be looking in," which the user can answer immediately and correctly, and which usually collapses the search to a single directory. This applies whenever an identifier the user owns (project, feature, ticket) can substitute for an identifier the machine owns (path, hash, filename).

The decision not to begin Task 4 records a judgment about work granularity under a resource ceiling. The task's shape — spawning implementer and reviewer subagents, per the two-stage review methodology in [[concepts/subagent-driven-development]] — means it consumes a long, uninterruptible run rather than decomposing into resumable increments. With the usage limit near, the two options were an unstarted task with a clean handoff, or a half-executed task whose partial state would need to be understood and possibly unwound by the next session. Choosing the former treats a clean boundary as more valuable than marginal progress, which is the correct trade when the work's own structure resists being resumed midway. It also parallels the closeout classification in [[concepts/machine-restore-closeout-handoff]], where items were sorted into finished, self-draining, and deliberately parked rather than all being pushed toward completion.

# SportScienceResearchRepo Batch PDF Import Pipeline

SportScienceResearchRepo maintains a `papers.json` database of sports-science research papers, built up through an ongoing batch-import campaign that processes a large backlog of football-related PDFs in rounds. On 2026-04-21, round 7 used 10 parallel subagents to add papers with IDs 334-383 to the database. A follow-up session on 2026-04-22 resolved a set of `year: 0`/blank-data quality issues left over from earlier rounds, including two that round 7 itself had flagged.

## Key Points

- Each import round assigns a contiguous block of IDs (round 7: 334-383, 50 papers) across 10 parallel subagents, with each agent handling a 5-paper batch.
- Before writing agent prompts for a new round, the format/schema is confirmed against a recently-completed batch file to keep entries consistent across rounds.
- Agents complete in non-sequential order; completions are tracked individually (round 7: agents 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 finished first, with agents 4, 6, and 10 still outstanding) before a separate "merge agent" consolidates all 10 batch files into `papers.json` and pushes the result.
- The `papers.json` schema includes a `"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE"` marker for entries whose source PDF cannot be located on disk, used for ID 358 (a KIAA0319 genetics paper) until it was resolved on 2026-04-22.
- On 2026-04-22, a repair session fixed 6 entries with `year: 0`/blank data carried over from earlier rounds: IDs 286 and 287 (true duplicates), 292 and 294 (unreadable filenames), 336 (a misassigned URL, recataloged from an ankle-sprain paper to Xia et al. 2024 on gut microbiota), and 358 (the KIAA0319 paper, originally blocked by non-breaking spaces in its filename) - resolving both of the data-quality issues round 7 had flagged (336 and 358).
- A background repair agent's proposed fixes (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`) contained hallucinated author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358; these were corrected via PyPDF2 text extraction directly from the source PDFs before committing, and round 8 was set to begin at ID 384 (~319 papers remaining across rounds 8-12).

## Details

The batch-import campaign works through a large backlog of football-related research PDFs in fixed-size rounds, each adding 50 papers via 10 parallel 5-paper agent batches. This parallelization lets a round's worth of extraction work happen concurrently, but it also means completion tracking has to happen at the individual-agent level - in round 7, seven of the ten agents (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9) finished before the remaining three (4, 6, 10), and the round could not be merged until all ten reported done. Once all batch files are complete, a dedicated merge agent consolidates them into the shared `papers.json` and pushes the update, advancing the repo's paper count (333 -> 383 after round 7).

Round 7 also surfaced several data-quality edge cases that the pipeline has conventions for handling rather than blocking on. ID 358 could not be matched to any PDF on disk and was marked `"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE"` per schema rather than skipped entirely. ID 336's source PDF had a curly apostrophe in its filename (URL-encoded as `%E2%80%99` in its `driveUrl`), which prevented the file from being read - this was logged as an open issue to investigate and fix rather than resolved inline. ID 343's PDF was misnamed "NFL Play Smart" but actually contained an unrelated hamstring-injury paper (Vermeulen et al.), requiring the agent to catalog it under its true content rather than its filename. ID 340 (Dupont et al., on lumbar disk herniation) used a Wolters Kluwer "in-press" DOI format whose final form was uncertain, so it was flagged for staff verification rather than guessed at. Together these conventions - explicit "unreadable" markers, content-based (not filename-based) cataloging, and flagging-for-review rather than guessing - keep the dataset complete and auditable even when individual source files are problematic.

The 2026-04-22 session closed out exactly the two issues round 7 had flagged - ID 358 (unreadable filename) and ID 336 (curly-apostrophe filename/misassigned URL) - alongside four additional `year: 0`/blank entries (286, 287, 292, 294) discovered separately. The session began by discovering that a previous session's background repair agent, which had produced a candidate fix file (`docs/batch_r7_fixes.json`), had not actually finished its work - so the fix was resumed from scratch rather than assumed complete. Worse, where the agent HAD produced output, its proposed citations for IDs 286, 287, and 358 had hallucinated author lists despite identifying the correct paper topics; for ID 336, the agent had also proposed the wrong replacement paper entirely (an ankle-sprain study) before the correct one (Xia et al. 2024, on gut microbiota) was identified. All three hallucinated citations were caught and corrected by extracting the actual text of the source PDFs with PyPDF2 (run via Bash) and re-citing from that verified text. The session also confirmed that non-breaking spaces and curly apostrophes embedded in PDF filenames - the root cause of IDs 358 and 336's original "unreadable" status - break Claude Code's `Read` tool, and that the practical workaround is PyPDF2 text extraction via Bash combined with exact byte-level filename inspection rather than retyping filenames by hand. A durable procedural lesson also emerged: always verify that a previous session's background agents actually completed before assuming their work is done, since the r7 repair agent had left its fix file incomplete.

# The .Codex Path Rewrite Incident in ~/.agents/skills

On 2026-08-08, a small-looking cleanup task — fixing a `.Codex` path bug in `~/.agents/skills` left over from the Windows→Mac migration — expanded into a repo-reconciliation and symlink-corruption incident. The bug was initially scoped at 29 files but proved to be 235 occurrences across 73 files. More consequentially, the upstream repository (`origin/main` of `erash11/claude-skills`) already had every path correct, meaning the local mass-edit was a redundant redo of work already done properly upstream; the real defect was a stale local checkout, not the paths.

## Key Points

- **Scope was underestimated ~8×:** the initial estimate of 29 affected files was wrong; the actual footprint was **235 occurrences across 73 files**, because the first survey missed several path shapes — `.Codex/LIFEOS/…`, `.Codex/global-memory/`, `.Codex/projects/`, and the Windows-style `~\.Codex\scripts\daily-backup.ps1`.
- **Upstream was already correct:** `origin/main` of `erash11/claude-skills` contained zero `.Codex` occurrences and zero Windows paths. The local checkout was 5 commits behind and missing 933 upstream files. Consulting git first would have made the entire rewrite unnecessary.
- **A blanket prose find-and-replace corrupted non-path text:** the original "Claude"→"Codex" substitution had been applied indiscriminately, mangling `claude.ai/design` → `Codex.ai/design` (×10 occurrences), Anthropic publication titles, and product references. Only `CLAUDE.md`→`AGENTS.md` was plausibly an intentional Codex port, creating genuine ambiguity about the original author's intent.
- **Case-sensitivity mattered twice:** the fix used `LC_ALL=C sed` specifically to preserve 13 legitimate lowercase `~/.codex` CLI references (in `impeccable/`, `watch/`, `claude-stack-doctor/`). Separately, macOS's case-insensitive filesystem hid the problem, because `.Codex` and `.codex` resolve to the same directory on disk.
- **Fix shipped as `6799781`** on the `claude-global-memory` repo; the subsequent `git reset --hard origin/main` on `~/.agents/skills` was the structurally correct remedy but triggered the symlink corruption documented separately.

## Details

The incident illustrates two compounding failure modes. The first is scope estimation from an incomplete survey: the initial grep pattern matched only the most obvious `.Codex` shape and missed several variants, including a Windows-backslash form (`~\.Codex\scripts\daily-backup.ps1`) that a POSIX-path-oriented pattern would never catch. Because migration artifacts inherit the path conventions of *both* the source and destination platforms, any survey of a Windows→Mac migration must enumerate both separator styles and both case variants before a count is trustworthy. On macOS this is further obscured by the case-insensitive filesystem: `.Codex` and `.codex` name the same directory, so the bug produced no filesystem-level error and could only be detected by reading text, not by testing whether paths resolved.

The second and more important failure mode is editing without first establishing ground truth. The local `~/.agents/skills` checkout was 5 commits behind `origin/main` and missing 933 files; upstream had already been migrated correctly. The 235-occurrence `sed` pass therefore reproduced, by hand and imperfectly, a correction that already existed in version control. The correct first move — `git fetch && git log origin/main` and a diff against the remote — would have reframed the task from "rewrite 73 files" to "sync a stale checkout." This is the central procedural lesson: **when a repository is under version control, check git before mass-editing**, because the remote is often authoritative and the local divergence is the actual defect.

The blanket prose substitution adds a third dimension. A find-and-replace of a *brand name* rather than a *path prefix* cannot distinguish structural references from prose, so it corrupted external URLs (`claude.ai/design`), publication titles, and product names alongside the intended path segments. The remediation had to be case-sensitive (`LC_ALL=C sed`) to avoid clobbering 13 legitimate lowercase `~/.codex` CLI references — the Codex CLI's own real config directory, which was never part of the bug. The general rule this yields: scope automated substitutions to the narrowest unambiguous token (a full path prefix with separators, not a bare word), and enumerate the legitimate occurrences you intend to preserve before running the pass.

# Zotero Research Library CLI (`zotero-research-library-pp-cli`)

A Zotero Research Library CLI tool, built as part of the printing-press project, was developed in waves on 2026-05-18. Waves 1–5 were completed in a single session, producing 32 source files, ~3,000 LOC, and 21 passing unit tests. The tool was validated against a real Zotero library (2,064 items, version 4500), during which a critical self-inflicted sync bug was discovered and fixed. On 2026-05-19, the working binary (`auth`, `doctor`, `sync`) was installed as the `/pp-zotero-research-library` v0.1 Claude Code slash command. On 2026-05-21, v0.1 was formally declared **functionally complete** after `sync --full` successfully ingested all 2,064 items in ~75 seconds, clearing the broken cached state left by the prior 304 bug. On 2026-08-06, the tool was carried through a publish pull request (**PR #1668**) that passed an 8-round Greptile review hardening its credential-store and incremental-sync internals.

## Key Points

- Architecture is wave-based: Wave 1 (CLI skeleton), Wave 2 (auth), Wave 3 (doctor), Wave 4 (SQLite+FTS5+WAL store + HTTP client with Zotero API quirks), Wave 5 (sync command); Waves 6–8 (search/read commands, write commands, metadata/SKILL.md) deferred.
- The `doctor` subcommand validates connectivity and exits with code 5 on failure; a bug was caught and fixed where JSON-output mode was incorrectly exiting 0 on failure (text mode had always exited 5 correctly).
- The SQLite store uses FTS5 for full-text search and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode for concurrent read access.
- **Critical sync bug discovered during testing:** the HTTP client auto-injected `If-Modified-Since-Version` as a header on all requests. During a sync run, the first `format=versions` call updated the stored library version to 4500, then subsequent batch-fetch calls sent that same version as a header — the server returned 304 Not Modified and zero items were upserted despite 2,064 items existing. Fix: remove auto-injection of this header; use only the `since=N` query param for incremental sync.
- **Recovery from broken cache:** after the 304 bug stored `last_version = 4500` before any items were actually fetched, the correct recovery is `sync --full` — which ignores the cached version and re-pulls the entire library. On 2026-05-21 this run completed successfully: 2,064 items ingested in approximately 75 seconds. This closed the last open question from the v0.1 milestone and the release was declared functionally complete.
- **BBT backfill constraint:** Better BibTeX citekey backfill requires the Zotero desktop application to be running during the sync; a sync run without Zotero desktop open will skip citekeys. This step was deferred.
- **v0.1 scope and slash command (2026-05-19):** the three working commands (`auth`, `doctor`, `sync`) were installed as `/pp-zotero-research-library` v0.1. The SKILL.md explicitly refuses all other commands as unimplemented. The full printing-press flow to add remaining features requires a dedicated interactive session (~30–60 min, ~5 checkpoints) where the user is present.
- **Publish review (PR #1668, 2026-08-06):** the tool was carried through a publish PR that passed an iterative Greptile review — 14 findings across 8 rounds — hardening the credential store (uniform `CredentialStorePath` routing, `https`/`zotero.org` API-key guard) and incremental sync (typed-table failures no longer advance the watermark, scalar deletion tombstones wrapped as storable `{"key": ...}` objects). See [[concepts/greptile-iterative-review-credential-consistency]].

## Details

The wave-based development model allowed each wave's completion to be validated independently before the next wave was started, with the `doctor --json` output against a real library serving as the first live integration check at the end of Wave 3. The SQLite store's choice of FTS5 and WAL reflects the tool's design as a local-first research assistant: FTS5 enables fast full-text search across all synced items without a search backend, while WAL allows concurrent reads from other processes (e.g., a separate query process) without blocking the sync writer.

The sync bug found during Wave 5 testing is the most operationally significant finding from the development session. The HTTP client had been designed defensively to auto-inject `If-Modified-Since-Version` on all requests, intending to avoid redundant re-fetches of unchanged data. In practice, within a single sync run, this was self-defeating: once the first API call updated the locally stored library version, all subsequent calls in the same run saw that version as a header and received 304s, making the sync appear to complete successfully while writing nothing. The root cause is a sequencing assumption mismatch — the header is appropriate for "nothing has changed since my last complete sync," but not for "I am mid-way through fetching data from a sync whose version I have just learned." This distinction is captured in detail in [[concepts/zotero-api-integration-reference]]. The practical recovery path — `sync --full` — ignores the cached version entirely and was confirmed to work correctly on 2026-05-21 (2,064 items, ~75 seconds), formally closing the v0.1 milestone.

On 2026-05-19, rather than running the full `/printing-press zotero` flow (which produces a comprehensive CLI covering all planned commands but requires live user attendance at ~5 checkpoints over 30–60 minutes), the existing Waves 1–5 binary was installed directly and a SKILL.md was hand-authored to honestly document the v0.1 scope. The SKILL.md explicitly states which commands are implemented and refuses all others with a clear "not yet implemented" message, avoiding silent failures for users who invoke the full command surface before it is built. The deferred full-scope work — search, add, items, collections, tags, BBT bridge, and bib export — is planned for a future interactive `/printing-press zotero` session where the user can attend each checkpoint live. See [[concepts/printing-press-cli-slash-commands]] for the broader context of that workflow constraint. On 2026-08-06 the tool reached a publish pull request (#1668); the accompanying Greptile review focused almost entirely on hardening the credential store and incremental-sync durability rather than user-facing commands, indicating the core data plane rather than the command surface was the review's risk center.

# In-Session Background Processes Don't Survive; Hours-Scale Work Belongs in Scheduled Jobs

Long-running background processes started from within a Claude Code session do not reliably survive the session — when the session ends they are terminated (status `killed`), and any child work they spawned can be left orphaned. On 2026-07-27, this was demonstrated when foreground memsearch reindex tasks were killed twice, leaving orphaned indexer processes that had to be cleaned up. The architectural conclusion: work measured in hours (like a first-time embedding index) belongs in a scheduled OS-level job, not an in-session background command.

## Key Points

- **Session-scoped processes are killed with the session:** a background command launched inside a session shares the session's lifetime; when the session terminates, the process is killed (observed status `killed`), regardless of whether its work completed.
- **Killed background jobs can orphan children:** the 2026-07-27 reindex tasks were killed twice, each time leaving orphaned indexer processes still holding CPU that had to be manually cleaned up — a killed parent does not guarantee a clean child teardown.
- **Hours-scale work must be relocated to a scheduled job:** a first-time SecondBrain book-library index is an hours-scale job (one indexer burned 81 CPU-minutes and was still going); the correct home is a Windows scheduled task (the 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1`), which runs independently of any session.
- **Sessions cannot wait through discontinuities:** a session cannot wait through a machine restart, nor block for hours on an index; the general workaround is to hand the work to a scheduled task and surface results/failures asynchronously (e.g., via `.errors.log` escalation read at the next session start).

## Details

The failure is structural, not incidental. A Claude Code session's process tree is tied to the session's lifetime, so any background command it launches is a candidate for termination when the session ends or is interrupted. This is acceptable for short tasks that finish within a turn, but it is fundamentally mismatched to work whose runtime exceeds a session — an hours-scale first-time embedding index cannot complete before the session that started it is likely gone. Worse, a killed background parent does not guarantee its own descendants are reaped: on 2026-07-27 the killed reindex tasks left orphaned indexer processes consuming CPU, requiring an explicit cleanup pass. The lesson is that the session is the wrong execution context for durable, long-running work.

The remedy is to move such work to an OS-level scheduler that owns its own lifetime and execution ceiling — in this case the nightly 6:15 AM backup task, which runs uncapped by the session, with an execution limit widened (30 min → 2 h) to absorb a heavy reindex night. This is the same reasoning that motivates the self-deleting post-restart health-check task: since a session cannot literally wait through a reboot, a logon-triggered scheduled task performs the post-restart verification and escalates failures asynchronously. In both cases the pattern is identical — take work that outlives or straddles a session boundary, hand it to a scheduled task, and reconcile the outcome later through a durable artifact (a log, an alarm counter, an escalation file) rather than expecting the session to hold state across the gap.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

# Connection: Background Task Exit-Code Failures Can Be False Positives

## The Connection

On 2026-07-18, the SpeedProfiling ticket-04 full-game data pull ran as a background R task that reported "failed / exit code 1," yet the task's own log showed a clean end-to-end run — the 10 Hz cache hit, 188 play-by-play plays saved, and the expected outputs written to disk (see [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]). This is a specific instance of a recurring class of tooling failure documented across the environment: a status/exit signal reporting failure that does not reflect the actual outcome, where the ground truth lives in a lower-level artifact (a log file, an on-disk output) rather than the reported status code.

## Key Insight

Exit codes and background-task status notifications are intermediate signals, not ground truth. A non-zero exit code from a detached or backgrounded process can be an artifact of the process-management layer (shell wrapper, harness notification, cleanup step) rather than a genuine failure of the work the process performed. The correct diagnostic response is to inspect the actual output — the log's final lines, the files on disk, the row counts — before treating the reported failure as real. On 2026-07-18 the SpeedProfiling pull's on-disk verification (8,932,931 rows for all 61/61 athletes, 69/69 tests passing, both caches confirmed hit on re-run) established the run had actually succeeded despite the exit-1 notification.

This mirrors the memsearch silent `exit 1` failure class (2026-06-13), where a memsearch invocation exited 1 with no surviving diagnostic output — the inverse problem, where a real failure left no trace and could not be diagnosed from the status alone. Together the two cases bracket the same lesson: the exit code and the actual outcome are independent signals that must be reconciled by examining the primitive artifacts. This is the process-execution analog of the broader "verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer" discipline: just as agent citations, preview-server renders, and retrieval scores can misrepresent ground truth, so can a process's reported exit status.

# Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology

On 2026-05-21, a structured 7-day retrospective (covering May 14–21) and a cold-project triage exercise were conducted to address project sprawl across many concurrent initiatives. The retrospective produced a structured cross-project summary of work completed and 7 open loops with next actions; the triage sorted cold projects into 4 buckets and shipped a decision-tracking HTML artifact at `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html`.

## Key Points

- **7-day retrospective format:** a structured recap of all projects touched in a rolling window, categorized by status, covering CLI development (Zotero, Catapult), 5 new skills installed, Fireflies setup, memory and Obsidian integration, token dashboard setup, and side fixes for May 14–21. Concluded with 7 identified open loops, each paired with a concrete next action.
- **Cold-project 4-bucket triage:** cold projects (not touched during the retrospective window) are sorted into: **Resume** (active work, blocked on a specific next action), **Decide** (uncertain whether to continue; needs a deliberate go/no-go decision), **Done** (formally closeable), **Archive/Kill** (permanently deprioritized or abandoned). The 2026-05-21 run sorted 16 projects: 3 resume, 2 decide, 3 done, 8 archive/kill.
- **Triage output artifact:** `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html` — a self-contained HTML file summarizing all bucketed projects with statuses and next actions, usable offline without re-running the triage.
- **Hottest cold project:** `Risk_Stratification_Engine` was flagged as the highest-priority cold project to resume next.
- **Project sprawl as a recurring pattern:** the user explicitly noted difficulty maintaining orientation across many concurrent initiatives; periodic retrospectives and triage dashboards were identified as the structural remedy.

## Details

The retrospective was triggered by the user explicitly losing track of what had been started, stopped, or left mid-flight — a common failure mode when many parallel workstreams run simultaneously across different tools, repositories, and roles. Rather than relying on memory or ad-hoc review, the session generated a structured cross-project summary covering the prior 7 days, making the "what exists and where it stands" question answerable in a single, deliberate pass. The format mirrors a lightweight sprint retrospective: scope (what was touched), status (done vs. in-flight vs. blocked), and open loops (concrete next actions, not vague intentions).

The 4-bucket triage model is designed to force explicit decisions rather than letting cold projects accumulate indefinitely in an ambiguous "maybe later" state. **Resume** identifies projects with a clear next action that are still worth pursuing. **Decide** surfaces projects that need a deliberate go/no-go call rather than being quietly ignored — the act of naming these forces a decision that passive neglect defers indefinitely. **Done** provides a formal closure signal for work that is genuinely complete but hasn't been officially closed. **Archive/Kill** handles deliberate deprioritization — not forgotten, but explicitly moved out of active consideration. The HTML artifact makes the triage durable and reviewable without accessing the session that produced it; sharing it as a file also separates the "what was triaged" question from the "what should I do next" question, allowing the artifact to be reviewed asynchronously.

The retrospective also surfaced a secondary benefit: completing deferred follow-up work from prior sessions. Specifically, the Zotero CLI's `sync --full` verification — left pending after the v0.1 slash command was registered on 2026-05-19 — was completed during the retrospective, with 2,064 items ingested successfully in ~75 seconds. Catching and completing loose ends like this is a natural output of a structured retrospective: open loops that were "almost done" become clearly visible and easy to close within the retrospective session itself.

# Morning Email Briefing System Design

On 2026-05-21, a design spec for an automated morning email briefing system was written and committed to `Desktop/DEV/morning-briefing/docs/2026-05-21-morning-briefing-design.md`. The system ingests email and calendar sources, distills them into a structured 6-section briefing, and delivers the result from Gmail to the user's work Outlook inbox at approximately 07:30 each morning. A durable markdown copy is saved to the SecondBrain vault regardless of delivery status. The implementation plan was started but not completed — the session hit its context-window limit mid-generation. On 2026-06-08, a full manual inbox audit validated the 6-section taxonomy against real Outlook inbox content, confirming the category distribution and the practical utility of separating FYI/newsletters from actionable sections.

## Key Points

- **Delivery config:** trigger at 07:20 so the briefing arrives ~07:30; send **from** `eric.rash11@gmail.com` **to** the user's work Outlook address (primary inbox). First-arrival junk-filter risk for Exchange tenants: `eric.rash11@gmail.com` should be added to safe-senders to prevent the first delivery being routed to junk by Exchange's external-sender heuristics.
- **6-section briefing format (all approved):** NEEDS REPLY, FOLLOW UPS, MEETINGS TO SCHEDULE, FORMS/TASKS OWED, STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS (age-tagged), FYI.
- **Live validation (2026-06-08):** a full manual Outlook inbox audit produced 50 categorized items: 11 needs_reply, 3 follow_ups, 3 meetings_to_schedule, 3 forms_owed, 6 still_open, 24 FYI/newsletters. The distribution confirms the design hypothesis — FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume (48%) but require no action, while actionable obligations are concentrated in a smaller set of items. See [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]].
- **No auto-learning:** the allowlist and mute list are manually curated only ("30 seconds a week"); automated pattern-learning was deliberately rejected to keep behavior predictable and auditable.
- **Graceful degradation:** the system must never silently skip a briefing — if a source fails, the briefing still sends with a banner explaining what could not be retrieved. Silent failures that leave the inbox empty are worse than a degraded briefing.
- **Durable markdown copy:** each day's briefing is saved to `Desktop/SecondBrain/morning-briefings/YYYY-MM-DD.md` regardless of email delivery outcome — the vault copy is a non-negotiable design requirement, not an optional log.
- **Self-review caught a spec gap:** a checklist self-review step during implementation plan generation identified that carryover items (STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS) were not being matched against today's new email threads for resolution detection — a behavioral omission in spec Section 8 that would have caused stale items to accumulate even after they were addressed in follow-up threads. The session hit the context-window limit while patching this gap, leaving the implementation plan incomplete.

## Details

The design spec's graceful-degradation principle is the most architecturally significant decision in the system. Making the briefing always send *something* — even a degraded version with a banner such as "⚠ Calendar source unavailable today" — is a conscious choice to prefer visible, annotated failures over silent ones. A pipeline that fails silently produces no signal that something broke; a degraded briefing with an explanatory banner tells the user what the system intended and why it could not fully deliver. This framing also means the implementation must treat each source (email, calendar, carryover state) as independently degradable — no single source failure should prevent the briefing from sending.

The self-review step during implementation plan generation caught a real behavioral defect in the spec before any code was written. The `writing-plans` skill includes a review checklist pass; that pass identified that the STILL OPEN section's carryover logic (spec Section 8) lacked a mechanism for detecting when a prior-day item had since been addressed by a new email thread — a gap that would have caused the carryover list to grow monotonically rather than shrinking as items were resolved. This is a planning-layer instance of the same principle documented in [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]]: a second review pass with a different focus (behavioral completeness rather than format compliance) catches what the initial drafting pass misses. Two items remain outstanding before implementation can proceed: the work Outlook email address (currently a placeholder in the spec), and completion of the implementation plan (left mid-write when the session expired).

The 2026-06-08 live inbox audit (see [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]]) validated the 6-section taxonomy against a real Outlook inbox. The distribution — 11 needs_reply, 3 follow_ups, 3 meetings_to_schedule, 3 forms_owed, 6 still_open, 24 FYI/newsletters — confirms that FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume (48%) but require no action, while actionable items are concentrated across the 5 actionable categories. This empirical validation supports the design decision to separate FYI from actionable sections rather than interleaving them. The same structured 6-category taxonomy drives both the manual triage process and this automated daily briefing, making the taxonomy the stable architectural element across both tools — see [[connections/inbox-triage-and-morning-briefing-taxonomy]].

# Skylar Zinnecker CMJ Return-to-Competition Reports

A series of CMJ (countermovement jump) force-plate performance reports were built for Baylor Athletics athlete Skylar Zinnecker on 2026-04-14, to support a return-to-competition (RTC) decision following injury and surgery. The reports were delivered as polished, print-ready HTML files using Chart.js, and were followed by a terminology cleanup and project documentation pass.

## Key Points

- Source data was a VALD ForceDecks export (`CMJ-test-export-04_14_2026.csv`, 67 sessions spanning August 2023-April 2026), processed into HTML reports with Chart.js visualizations.
- Injury (April 12, 2025) and surgery (April 25, 2025) dates were annotated as vertical markers on the charts.
- The baseline was redefined from a full 2-year historical average to the last 4 pre-injury sessions (March 20-April 10, 2025) - a clinically more appropriate baseline for an RTC assessment - while "current" values used a 3-session rolling average from April 2, 7, and 8, 2026.
- The baseline change flipped the Lower-Limb Stiffness metric's status from "Progressing" (⚠) to "Exceeds Baseline" (✓), since the new baseline (4,693) was lower than the old one (5,477); asymmetry metrics were normalized inversely (lower % = better) for the radar chart.
- The term "nadir"/"Injury Nadir" (the post-surgery performance floor used in the recovery-percentage formula) was replaced with the clinically clearer "Post-Op Low" across all three HTML files (9 instances total), after the user found "nadir" too jargon-heavy for a clinical audience.

## Details

Styling followed Baylor's institutional branding (`#1e4d2b` green, `#b87d0a` gold) in light mode, with full print CSS (`@page` set to letter portrait, plus `-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact` to preserve colors when printed).
